name: The mutual dependence of Pope and Emperor
plain_explanation: After Charlemagne's coronation in 800, no one could legitimately become Holy Roman Emperor without being crowned by the Pope in Rome, but for centuries every strong emperor also claimed the right to appoint or depose popes. Neither office could fully dominate the other, so the two were locked in a relationship of galling but, for centuries, unavoidable mutual need.
precise_definition: Russell's account of the medieval theory of legitimate authority as resting jointly on Pope and Emperor: the Emperor derives legitimacy from papal coronation, while the Pope's temporal security and much of his authority historically depended on imperial protection and patronage.
why_it_mattered: This structural interdependence produced centuries of recurring conflict (culminating in the Investiture Controversy and the thirteenth-century struggles covered in later chapters), and its final breakdown in the fifteenth century -- through the rise of national monarchies and the Reformation -- ended the medieval unity of Christendom.
historical_origin: Begins with Charlemagne's coronation by Pope Leo III on Christmas Day, A.D. 800, itself made possible by Charlemagne's legal fiction that the imperial throne was vacant because the reigning Eastern sovereign, Irene, could not be Emperor as a woman.
examples: Charlemagne deriving his claim to legitimacy from the Pope while also protecting and effectively controlling the papacy
The later, more extreme conflict between Pope and Emperor culminating at Canossa (covered in Chapter IX)
influence_on_later_thinkers: Sets up the entire Guelf-Ghibelline conflict and the investiture disputes treated in Chapters IX through XII.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: This is itself a claim about the fusion of religious and secular legitimacy in medieval political theory.
